title: Not inflamed
hookLine: not knowing the eye as it is, one is inflamed; knowing it, one is free

cards: A bakery window at the end of a long day. Glazed pastries under warm light, a cake with a perfect swirl. The glass hasn't changed since morning, and the person walking past hadn't wanted cake a minute ago.
Now there's heat, a pull, a little restlessness. The hundred and forty-ninth discourse has a word for that state. The Pali is saratta, usually rendered inflamed, or impassioned.
And it says the fire doesn't start in the cake or the window. It starts in how things are seen.

teach.b: The discourse is called the great six sense bases, and it begins with a contrast.

When someone doesn't know and see the eye as it actually is, the Buddha says, and doesn't know forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact and the feeling that comes from it as they actually are, they become inflamed by lust for all of it.
Inflamed, tied up, infatuated, fixed on the sweetness. Then things build. Craving grows.
The heaps of clinging pile up for the future.
Troubles of body and mind grow, torments grow, fevers grow, and the person feels it, in body and in mind. Now the other side.
When someone knows and sees the eye, the forms and the seeing as they actually are, they aren't inflamed. Craving fades. The heaps of clinging shrink.
The fevers go down. And this person, the text says, feels ease, in body and in mind. The key phrase is yathabhuta: as it actually is.
Not as advertised, not as feared. Notice what's not being blamed. Not the eye.
Not the world. The eye is fine. The cake is fine.
The problem is the fog between them. Then a surprise. For a person who sees this way, the text says, their view simply is right view, their intention right intention, their effort right effort.
The eightfold path comes to fulfillment in them.
Calm and insight, it says, run together, evenly yoked. Like two oxen under one yoke, pulling one cart.

how: Theravada meditators practice sense restraint and bare noticing, seeing what comes through each sense as it actually is; teachers often pair this with calm practice so that, as MN 149 says, calm and insight develop together.

o: not set on fire by the pull of what's seen
free from fever after an illness

s: MN 149 says the eye itself is the problem
the eye is fine. the problem is not knowing it, and what it sees, as it actually is.
the text says clear seeing brings ease in body and mind
fevers and torments go down, and the person feels ease.
for someone who sees clearly, the eightfold path is said to come to fulfillment
their view simply is right view, their effort right effort, and so on.

games.q: a beautiful thing catches your eye and the old heat starts to rise. what does MN 149 point to?
o: see the eye, the thing and the feeling as they actually are.
never look at anything beautiful again.
get the thing quickly so the heat stops.
games.why: the discourse doesn't ask anyone to close their eyes. it asks them to see clearly, and says the inflaming fades when they do.

practice: Rest one hand on something near you, a sleeve, a table, your knee, and feel just texture and temperature.

Notice whether there's a small liking or disliking, a pull toward it or away, and without fixing it, name it: liking, not liking, or neither. Then let the hand go still, and notice the temperature of the mind: warm, cool, still?

wordCard.voice: Not inflamed. Seeing the senses as they actually are, yathabhuta, so the pull of what's seen doesn't set the mind on fire. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali yathabhuta: as it actually is, as it has come to be. the key to not being inflamed.

carryVoice: Your line: two oxen under one yoke. The cake was never the problem; the fog is what clears. That's day five hundred fourteen.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 149, Mahasalayatanika Sutta (the great discourse on the six sense bases)
